extracted.intended_audience: academic economists, financial economists, and policy researchers studying climate-economy interactions and the social cost of carbon
extracted.subtask_description: Using forward-looking capital-market data and a temperature-augmented long-run risks model (LRR-T) to estimate the economic impact of long-run temperature shifts, price temperature risk, and quantify the social cost of carbon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of forward-looking equity prices to infer long-horizon temperature effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward-looking equity prices that are determined by the discounted value of future growth rates provide important information about the cost of long-horizon temperature fluctuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the implication that temperature risks have a measurable impact on current equity valuations to estimate the price of temperature risks; focus on asset prices (e.g., price-dividend ratios, consumption claims) rather than historical GDP alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling framework — LRR-T (temperature-augmented long-run risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Build on the long-run risks framework of Bansal and Yaron (2004) and account for temperature-induced natural disasters in future output and growth; temperature is a source of economic risk that affects expected growth rates and discount rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate disasters triggered when temperature breaches a threshold (tipping point); model interaction between climate change, economic growth and risk so both cash-flow and discount-rate channels operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature and emissions dynamics specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions: Et = Ct^{λ_t} (log growth ∆e_{t+1} = λ_{t+1} ∆c_{t+1} + ∆λ_{t+1} c_t). Temperature: T_t = ν_t T_{t-1} + χ e_t, where ν_t ∈ (0,1) is carbon retention and χ>0 is sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibrate carbon intensity path (λ_t) and temperature (T_t) to match BAU (Nordhaus 2010) and IPCC forecasts; allow ν_t to increase with carbon intensity to capture reinforcing feedbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaster trigger and damage functional forms (tipping point specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural disasters are triggered when temperature reaches a tipping point T*: both occurrence (intensity π_t) and expected size (d_t) of disasters are increasing in temperature. Use guarded functional forms: d_t = q1 T_t + q2 T_t^2 (if T_t ≥ T*), π_t = l0 + l1 T_t (if T_t ≥ T*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model disasters with a compensated compound Poisson process (Dt+1 = sum ζ_i,t+1 − d_t π_t), with gamma-distributed jumps; choose quadratic loss functions consistent with climate literature (Nordhaus, Weitzman, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumption growth and propagation of disaster effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumption growth follows ∆c_{t+1} = μ + x_t + σ η_{t+1} − D_{t+1}; x_{t+1} = ρ_x x_t + φ_x σ ε_{t+1} − ϕ_x D_{t+1}. Disasters affect growth (permanent effect) via D_{t+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume disasters reduce future consumption growth (permanent effect) and propagate through persistence in long-run risk component; set parameters so the first-order autocorrelation of consumption growth (absent disasters) matches data (e.g., ~0.44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference specification and importance of timing of resolution of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Epstein–Zin (recursive) preferences (Ut defined recursively with parameters δ, γ, ψ). Preferences for early resolution of uncertainty (γ ≥ 1/ψ) are critical; power utility is the special case when γ = 1/ψ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of preference parameters (risk aversion γ, IES ψ, discount δ) strongly affects the discount-rate channel and therefore the social cost of carbon and sign of price-elasticities; compare recursive preferences to CRRA (power utility) as robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and computation of the Social Cost of Carbon (SCC)
rubrics_metrics.description: SCC_t = −(∂U_t / ∂E_t) / (∂U_t / ∂C_t). Equivalently SCC_0 = (ψ/(ψ−1)) (−∂Z_0/∂E_0 / Z_0) C_0, i.e., SCC equals monetized value of percent change in wealth due to an additional unit of emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute SCC in units of consumption goods by scaling marginal utility of emissions by marginal utility of consumption; SCC depends on both cash-flow (damage) effects and discount-rate (preference) effects, so calibrate to match asset-market discount rates when using market data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration targets and choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibrate carbon intensity and temperature path to BAU forecasts (Nordhaus 2010) and IPCC; set tipping point T* = 2°C; time measured in decades with steady state in 60 periods; assume ~80% of current CO2 remains for another century (average retention ~0.962).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose preference and consumption dynamics parameters to match key financial moments: e.g., γ=5, ψ=1.5, δ=0.99, μ=1.8% annual consumption growth, σ shocks 1.6% annual, consumption autocorrelation ~0.44, exposure of expected growth to disasters 0.05. Calibrate disaster probabilities/sizes conservatively (e.g., upon crossing 2°C annual disaster prob ~1.2% rising to 2.8%, avg losses −0.7% to −6%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction: price of low-frequency (long-run) temperature risk increases with temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Model predicts that the price of low-frequency temperature risks and their risk premia increase with temperature (∂λ_D(T_t)/∂T_t < 0 and the temperature beta magnitude increases with T_t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test this implication empirically by allowing for time-varying price of temperature risk (e.g., include interaction terms with level of temperature) and by examining different horizons (1-, 5-, 10-year moving averages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measurement of temperature exposure (temperature beta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate exposure of portfolio/asset returns to temperature fluctuations by regressing excess returns on the change in K-year moving average of temperature (e.g., K = 1, 5, 10), controlling for market and consumption growth risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute temperature betas for cross-sectional assets (25 BM/size portfolios; industry portfolios); include controls for market and consumption risk in the first-stage regression to isolate temperature exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-sectional pricing test to estimate price of temperature risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the market price of temperature risk by regressing average excess returns on estimated temperature betas (and other factor betas) using Fama–MacBeth cross-sectional regressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Fama–MacBeth t-statistics and apply Shanken (1992)-corrected t-statistics; evaluate significance with Monte Carlo p-values generated under the null that temperature risks have no effect on equity prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and asset grouping choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a cross-section of 25 book-to-market and size-sorted portfolios and 10 industry portfolios for US analyses (annual data, e.g., 1934–2014); for international panel use up to 39 countries (1970–2012 or 1980–2009 depending on specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify industries by heat exposure (e.g., National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health classification) and exclude countries with missing controls in panel regressions; report sample periods and any exclusions explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical adjustments and inference details
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Shanken (1992)-corrected t-statistics for cross-sectional factor pricing tests; report Monte Carlo p-values for the fraction of simulated samples under the null with corrected t-statistics less than sample statistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also report conventional t-stats; provide adjusted R^2; for panel regressions use robust standard errors (White) and appropriate GMM estimators (Arellano–Bond) when dynamic panels and fixed effects are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel regression specification for international evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate panel regression vi,t = v̄_i + ϕ^K T^K_{i,t} + α'x X_{i,t} + α_v v_{i,t−1} + ε_{i,t}, where v is log price-dividend ratio, T^K is K-year moving-average temperature, X includes global and local controls (two price-dividend factors, inflation, unemployment, real interest rate, GDP growth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate via Arellano–Bond GMM on first-differenced data; report slope coefficient ϕ^K and White-robust t-statistics; test robustness across sample windows (e.g., 1980–2000, 1980–2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition into long-run and short-run temperature components
rubrics_metrics.description: Proxy low-frequency temperature risks by K-year moving averages (LR_K) and short-run risks by the annual component orthogonalized with respect to long-run fluctuations (SR). Regress price-dividend on both LR and SR simultaneously to identify which drives equity responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect long-run (trend) component to have larger negative effect on valuations; report estimates and t-statistics for both components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-varying price specification (interaction with temperature level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow price of temperature risk to vary with the level of temperature by including terms such as (T_t × ∆T_{t+1}) in cross-sectional regressions (estimate ˆλ_{∆T} and ˆλ_{T·∆T}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the price of temperature risk increases (in magnitude) with T_t; present Shanken-corrected t-stats and Monte Carlo p-values for these coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: VAR and impulse-response analysis for dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a panel VAR (e.g., first-order) for equity prices and temperature (use moving averages and annual series) including exogenous controls to compute impulse responses of price-dividend ratios to long- and short-run temperature shocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report VAR coefficient estimates, t-statistics, and R^2; present impulse responses with standard error bands to show persistence and magnitude of equity-price responses to shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping consumption-claim price responses to equity price responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the model-implied elasticity of the price-consumption (wealth-consumption) ratio to temperature and adjust by economy/market leverage (e.g., market leverage ~3) to translate consumption-claim responses into equity price responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare model-implied elasticity (e.g., −0.87% price-consumption for 0.5°C increase) with empirical estimates (after accounting for leverage) as a validation check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical solution and approximation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve the model numerically using value function iteration, discretize the state space, and use Chebyshev polynomial approximation of the value/policy function; start at a terminal date where temperature anomaly disappears and work backwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure time horizon and discretization are sufficient to reach steady state; report numerical methods and convergence diagnostics.
